name: Tokugawa Japan
title: Social Hierarchy of Tokugawa Japan: From Emperor to Outcasts

tiers.name: The emperor and the court nobles
tiers.term: kinri (the emperor and his palace), kuge (court nobles)
tiers.you: You belong to the imperial court in Kyoto, among the most honoured families in Japan, but the shogun’s deputy oversees the court, and you earn part of your living by teaching poetry or music to paying pupils.
tiers.kid: The emperor lived in Kyoto and was greatly honoured, but the shogun, not the emperor, ruled Japan.
tiers.rise: Birth decided everything: the throne passed within the imperial family, and court offices within the kuge houses by the rank of each house. The court went on granting ranks to the daimyo, but only on the shogunate’s recommendation.
tiers.why: Highest in honour stood the emperor in Kyoto.

tiers.name: The shogun
tiers.you: You rule Japan from Edo in the emperor’s name: you confirm or remove the daimyo, keep their families in your capital and decide on foreign affairs and coinage, though the emperor in Kyoto still outranks you in honour.
tiers.kid: The shogun was Japan’s real ruler, a general from the Tokugawa family who governed from the city of Edo.
tiers.rise: The office passed within the Tokugawa house, to an heir from a branch house when the main line failed, as in 1716. Ieyasu meant to close the road by which Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the son of peasants, had risen to rule Japan a generation earlier.
tiers.why: The shogun was the real ruler of Japan.

tiers.name: Daimyo
tiers.you: You rule a domain of at least 10,000 koku with your own samurai and laws, but every other year you must go to Edo, where your wife and children live as the shogun’s hostages.
tiers.kid: Daimyo were great lords who ruled parts of Japan for the shogun and had to live in his city every other year.
tiers.rise: A daimyo’s son or adopted heir succeeded him with the shogun’s approval. The shogun could make a loyal retainer a daimyo by granting him more land, or reduce, move or abolish a domain, as he often did in the early decades of the period.
tiers.why: Below the shogun stood the daimyo, the lords of about 260 to 270 domains (han), each assessed at 10,000 koku of rice or more; the greatest, the Maeda of Kaga, held about a million.

tiers.name: Samurai
tiers.you: You wear two swords and draw a rice stipend from your lord, and you serve him as an official or guard in his castle town; you may not farm or trade, and your stipend may not cover your debts.
tiers.kid: Samurai were warriors who wore two swords, and in the long Edo peace most of them worked as officials and guards.
tiers.rise: Status passed from father to son, or to an adopted son, and a talented man could rise only a few steps above his birth. From the 18th century rich commoners bought their way in by paying a poor retainer of the shogun to adopt a son; a samurai who lost his lord became a masterless rōnin.
tiers.why: The samurai were the hereditary warrior class, perhaps 400,000 men.

tiers.name: Buddhist and Shinto clergy
tiers.you: You serve a Buddhist temple to which every household of the neighbourhood must belong: you register its families each year, certify that none of them is a Christian, and live on the fees for funerals and memorial services.
tiers.kid: Buddhist priests looked after temples and kept a record of every family that belonged to them.
tiers.rise: Men of any class could take the robe. The samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo became a monk in 1700, when his lord died and retainers were forbidden to follow their lord in death.
tiers.why: Buddhist monks and priests and the priests of Shinto shrines stood outside the four classes.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You farm rice with your family, hand over close to half the harvest in tax, and need a permit to travel beyond your village.
tiers.kid: Most people in Edo Japan were farmers who grew rice and paid a large share of it to their lord.
tiers.rise: Peasant status passed with the household, though young people sometimes went to work outside the village for a season. A rich peasant family could buy a samurai adoption for a son, and some peasants’ sons won samurai status by serving in the office of a shogunal intendant (daikan); debt and famine pushed others into the towns’ poor or even among the hinin.
tiers.why: Four people in five were peasants (hyakushō), the villagers who grew the rice on which the whole order rested.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.you: You live in the craftsmen’s quarter of a castle town and make goods for samurai households and townspeople; in law you rank with the peasants and merchants, below every samurai.
tiers.kid: Artisans in Edo Japan made things like cooking pots, clothes, toys and books, mostly in the towns.
tiers.rise: Artisans belonged to the townspeople, whose wealthier members could buy a samurai adoption for a son from the 18th century. Movement also ran the other way: a low-ranking samurai could step down into a town trade.
tiers.why: In the four-class scheme the artisans (shokunin) came third, after the peasants, as makers of useful things.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You trade rice or lend money in Osaka or Edo and may be richer than the samurai who borrow from you, but the law forbids you to show your wealth and gives you no way to make a lord repay.
tiers.kid: Merchants were ranked low in theory, but many became very rich by trading rice and lending money.
tiers.rise: Wealth could not buy rank directly, but it opened other doors. A merchant’s daughter who married into a samurai family brought it money and her own family standing, a rich merchant could buy a samurai adoption for a son, and merchants who served as a domain’s financial agents received rice stipends and some samurai privileges.
tiers.why: Merchants stood last in the Confucian scheme, regarded as parasites who lived off others’ work, yet they became the richest commoners in Japan, and many were richer than the samurai who borrowed from them.

tiers.name: Outcasts of the leather trades
tiers.term: eta (the official term, now a slur)
tiers.you: You belong to a segregated kawata community: you tan hides or work the land, may be called on to guard prisoners, and must keep to rules on dress and movement that mark you as an outcast.
tiers.kid: Kawata families did jobs such as leatherwork that others thought unclean, and they were made to live apart.
tiers.rise: There was almost no way out: kawata status was inherited and permanent, and the rules of the 18th century made it harder still to leave. Records show that some nevertheless left their communities by flight.
tiers.why: The kawata, called eta in official documents (a term now a slur), were hereditary outcasts.

tiers.name: Outcasts of the streets
tiers.you: You live in the hinin quarter, beg or perform in the streets and are called on to clean the town or guard prisoners; if you fell to this status as a commoner, your relatives may still buy you back.
tiers.kid: Hinin were very poor outcasts who begged, performed in the streets and did jobs such as cleaning the towns.
tiers.rise: A hinin born to the status rarely left it, but one who had fallen into it could be restored to commoner status if the conditions were met, and the Kyōhō reforms made even this much harder.
tiers.why: The hinin, literally “non-people”, were outcasts of another kind.
